payload.because: The upgrade is provably invisible to everything sofar ships. tsc is used in exactly two places — noEmit typechecking and the L2 declaration emit in build.mjs — and never touches the esbuild bundles that are the actual published artifact, so all three JS bundles plus every runtime file hashed identical. The only delta is cosmetic: TS 7 preserves the source quote style in emitted string-literal types, so three d.ts files render readonly ['pass', 'findings'] where TS 6 rendered readonly ["pass", "findings"]. Those are the same type; no consumer can observe the difference. The config was already on the favorable side of the port — ES2022, ESNext, Bundler resolution, strict, noUncheckedIndexedAccess, isolatedModules, skipLibCheck, nothing legacy for the native compiler to reject. One behavioural difference found and worth knowing: TS 7 enforces forceConsistentCasingInFileNames against the invocation path where TS 6 normalised it away, so running tsc through a differently-cased path than the repo's canonical one (/Users/jins/io vs /Users/jins/IO on a case-insensitive macOS volume) raises TS1149 on files reached by relative import rather than through the workspace symlink. That is an invocation-path artifact, not a code defect: npm run typecheck runs from the package directory and is clean. Note the speedup is build- and editor-time only — it does nothing for the 26ms CLI hot path, which is Node executing esbuild output.
payload.chose: Upgrade the root devDependency typescript 6.0.3 to ^7.0.2, the native Go compiler port. Running the npm script is unaffected. dist is gitignored so no build output is committed. Initiative created without binding the branch, so main stays on session-driver for the peer session working 1.3.

payload.text: Record-hygiene D1 exempts a Bash call only when EVERY shell segment leads with git or sofar. Decorating a git command with echo labels — the common `echo "=== status ===" && git status` habit — breaks the exemption, so the PostToolUse hook appends a command_run event and the tree is dirty again the instant it was clean. This is exactly the loop D1 was written to break, and it is easy to re-enter by accident right after a write-back, where the trailing event lands after session_ended and forces an amend. Convention: once you have written back, run git and sofar commands BARE and chained only to each other (`git add <paths> && git commit --amend --no-edit`), with no echo, no comments and no pipes to head. Use echo decoration freely before the write-back, never after it.

payload.summary: Updated the runtime-comparison artifact (same URL, ff9f4ee7) to reflect the TypeScript 7.0.2 upgrade shipped in 87c4619, and answered two follow-up questions in it: why people write CLIs in Rust or Zig if TypeScript is fine, and how sofar scales. Added the TS 7 finding as the lead item, a Compiler speed row to the matrix, and two sections. The CLI section reframes the question away from the CLI category toward four discriminators that ripgrep, fd, uv and ruff all answer the opposite way sofar does: whether users already have the runtime (sofar users all do, Claude Code requires Node), whether the work is CPU-bound (sofar folds 10,460 JSON records and waits on write), whether it runs in a hot loop (once per hook at 26ms, not per keystroke), and whether a library surface ships alongside (sofar ships three JS entry points plus a browser bundle). Supporting point: the JS ecosystem already split along exactly that CPU-bound line — esbuild, swc, oxc, ruff and now tsc 7 went native while npm, pnpm, wrangler and the Vercel CLI stayed JS, because orchestration waits on IO. The scalability section states the real ceiling rather than dismissing it: the fold is O(n) per invocation, roughly 20-25ms of work at 10,460 events once node boot is subtracted, so about 250ms at 100k and 2.5s at a million, and that ceiling arrives in any language. A rewrite buys a constant factor while the ceiling is algorithmic. Grounded in this repo's own prior finding, quoted from the header comment of core/index-tier1.ts: buildGraph re-derives the whole graph at ~16ms and growing with history, and the way out is not a faster graph build but a different shape — the persisted keyed index with INDEX_SCHEMA_VERSION that turns sweeps into lookups. The scaling fix was already written in TypeScript and already shipped.
